questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old with a chronic condition wants his mother involved in the discussion of a non-urgent treatment because she helps him remember details, but he also wants the clinician to make sure the decision is based on **his own** understanding. What is the **best interpretation** based on the notes?

options.text: If a parent remains involved, the adolescent’s own competence no longer needs assessment
Support from a parent can still be helpful, but the consent assessment must still focus on the young person’s own capacities
Parental involvement automatically gives the parent final legal control of the decision
A valid consent discussion can only occur if the parent is completely excluded
The young person’s own view matters only if the parent disagrees with the doctor

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes define legal competence to consent by looking at the **minor’s** maturity, intelligence, experience, understanding, and ability to weigh risks, benefits, and longer-term impacts. That means a supportive parent may still be present or helpful, but the assessment of competence must still focus on the young person’s own capacities.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes assess competence through the minor’s own capacities, so parental involvement does not remove the need for that assessment.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not say that parental involvement automatically gives the parent final legal decision-making authority.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not require total parental exclusion for a consent discussion to be valid.
why_others_wrong.E: The young person’s own capacities matter throughout the assessment, not only if disagreement occurs.

key_takeaways: Consent assessment focuses on the young person’s own capacities.
Parental support and adolescent decision-making are not mutually exclusive.
Helpful family involvement does not replace assessment of the minor’s understanding.

questions.stem_markdown: Two siblings attend elective treatment counselling in a Sydney service. One is **17 years** old and the other has just turned **18 years** old. Both communicate well. Why does the clinician start from a different legal presumption in the older sibling?

options.text: Because adults are presumed competent to consent, whereas a minor’s competence must be determined rather than presumed
Because 18-year-olds can no longer refuse treatment
Because once a patient turns 18, consent from parents is always still required as backup
Because competence assessment is only relevant in emergencies for minors
Because a 17-year-old is automatically incompetent to make medical decisions

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that in Australia, anyone below age 18 is a **minor**, while an **adult (18 years and over) is presumed competent** to consent to medical treatment. This creates a different starting presumption for the 18-year-old, even though both patients may communicate well.

why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not say that adults lose the ability to refuse treatment.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material says adults are presumed competent; it does not say parental consent is still always required for adults.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes discuss competence assessment more broadly than emergency care alone.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not describe all 17-year-olds as automatically incompetent.

key_takeaways: Turning 18 changes the default legal presumption about competence.
A minor may still be competent, but that competence is not automatically presumed in the same way as adulthood.
Clinical communication can be similar across ages even when the legal starting point differs.

questions.stem_markdown: In a NSW consent-planning meeting, the consultant says a **16-year-old** is "a **young person**, not a child, but still a minor" according to the notes. The parents ask what that wording actually means in practice. What is the **best explanation**?

options.text: It means the patient is legally an adult for medical treatment decisions
It means the notes distinguish 16- to 17-year-olds from those 15 or younger, while both remain under the broader category of minor
It means the terms child and young person are interchangeable and have no relevance in the consent notes
It means only young people, but not children, can ever be assessed for competence
It means parental views no longer matter once the term young person is used

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes specifically state that, in the NSW material being summarised, a **child** is someone **15 or younger** and a **young person** is someone aged **16 or 17**. Both groups still sit within the broader category of **minor** because adulthood begins at 18.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes still describe a 16-year-old as a minor, not as an adult.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material explicitly distinguishes the terms rather than treating them as interchangeable.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not say that competence assessment applies only to one of these two subgroups.
why_others_wrong.E: The wording distinguishes categories within minority, but it does not say parental views become irrelevant.

key_takeaways: The notes use NSW wording that separates child from young person within the broader category of minor.
A 16-year-old is still a minor even though the notes use a different label from child.
Applied consent questions may depend on understanding how categories are defined in the notes.

questions.stem_markdown: A team has already determined that a proposed intervention for a **15-year-old** falls within the notes’ category of **special medical treatment**. The adolescent and both parents all agree and ask to sign the usual consent paperwork that day. What is the **best response**?

options.text: Ordinary parental consent is enough because there is agreement
The young person can consent alone if they appear mature
This category follows a different pathway, requiring consent from the Guardianship Division of NCAT rather than ordinary parental or mature-minor consent
No formal consent pathway is needed if everyone believes the treatment is beneficial
The special pathway matters only when the family disagrees

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that for **special medical treatment (<16 years old)**, **consent from the Guardianship Division of NCAT is required** and that **neither the parent nor the Mature Minor can consent**. Agreement within the family therefore does not convert it into an ordinary consent process.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes state that ordinary parental consent is not sufficient for this treatment category.
why_others_wrong.B: The source material says mature-minor consent is also not sufficient for this category.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not remove the formal pathway simply because the treatment is thought beneficial.
why_others_wrong.E: The special pathway depends on the treatment category, not merely on whether disagreement exists.

key_takeaways: Special medical treatment follows a distinct consent pathway in the notes.
Family agreement does not by itself make ordinary consent sufficient for this category.
Recognising an unusual consent pathway is part of applied adolescent care.
